To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) we identify a number of putative natural SP for GroEL and Hsp60 and (2) the number of natural SP is a function of the NC and NB.
we identify a number of putative natural SP sequences for GroEL and the analog Hsp60, and we show that a number of proteins can be substrates for chapperonins.
we have identified a number of natural SP sequences and their binding regions in E. coli and S.cerevisiae, using a sequence‐ based method.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a systematic analysis of the binding sites of natural SPs for the GroEL chaperonin.
the prediction of SPs for GroES and GroEL.
the identification of the natural SPs of GroEL, which will help in understanding the role of GroEL in vivo and the evolution of GroEL.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the GroEL machinery is a general folding catalyst, assisting the folding of a large number of proteins in vivo.
GroEL is an essential component of cellular machinery that assists in the folding of a variety of proteins.
GroEL can assist the folding of a large variety of proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GroEL is a highly versatile molecular chaperone.
the GroEL machinery can interact with a large number of proteins, and the interaction can be specific or nonspecific.
GroEL has a broad substrate specificity, and that its role is not limited to assisting the folding of a few proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the chaperonin‐binding regions are not limited to any particular secondary structure, and the interaction of SPs with the chaperonins is a function of both NC and NB.
the sequence‐based approach can be used to identify natural substrates for other chaperonins as well as for other protein‐binding proteins.
the chaperonins can interact with proteins that have diverse sequences.
